name: Pyritinol

lead: Pyritinol is a semi-synthetic compound made by linking two vitamin B6 molecules, produced by Merck in 1961. People take it as a nootropic for memory, focus and mental performance.

It is approved in several European countries for chronically impaired brain function in dementia syndromes, and in the US it has been sold as a supplement since the early 1990s. Human trials are mostly old and small with mixed results, and none address appearance.

paras: Taken orally as a nootropic supplement, usually as part of a study or work stack. Users generally treat it as a short-run cognitive aid.

Common effects are nausea and headache; mild skin allergy is rare. Case reports describe severe cholestatic hepatitis in patients on several drugs, acute pancreatitis, a photoallergic eruption and induced pemphigus. It is not recognised as a drug by the FDA.

angle.text: Pyritinol is taken as a nootropic for sharper memory and focus. It is approved in several European countries for dementia-related impairment, and its trials are mostly older cognition studies, with nothing on appearance.

lead: Pyritinol, also called pyrithioxine or pyridoxine disulfide, is a semi-synthetic, water-soluble compound made by joining two vitamin B6 (pyridoxine) molecules with a disulfide bridge. It was first produced by Merck in 1961, has been sold as a prescription and over-the-counter drug in several countries since the 1970s, and has been sold as a nootropic supplement in the United States since the early 1990s [1].

In the context of appearance, pyritinol sits at the edge of the topic. It appears in nootropic stacks on bodybuilding forums such as T Nation, where users describe it as a source of calm focus for work, study and training sessions; the supposed route to better looks is through consistency and concentration in the gym, diet and routine [2][3]. This is a user claim, and no trial measures appearance outcomes.

Approved uses are in medicine: several European countries license it for symptomatic treatment of chronically impaired brain function in dementia syndromes and for sequelae of head trauma, and France also approves it for rheumatoid arthritis [1]. Research is largely from the 1970s to 1990s, with small randomised trials in elderly patients, brain injury and healthy volunteers.
infobox: Approved in several EU states; sold as a supplement in the US

paras: Approved indications in Austria, Germany, France, Italy, Portugal and Greece include symptomatic treatment of chronically impaired brain function in dementia syndromes and supportive treatment after craniocerebral trauma. France also approves it as a disease-modifying drug in rheumatoid arthritis, and it has been used for learning disorders in children [1]. A 1995 German geriatrics review discussed it among the options and limits of therapy for cognition disorders in the elderly [4].

Posts on T Nation show pyritinol in multi-ingredient nootropic stacks, including commercial products listing it with vinpocetine, centrophenoxine, aniracetam and others [2][3]. One user who added it to a vinpocetine, choline and piracetam stack described calm focus alongside quickly developing tolerance [2]. Others recommend it to people with attention problems as a lesser-known option [5].

In a 1994 trial, 40 patients with probable Alzheimer's disease received social support, cognitive training alone, or cognitive training with pyritinol or phosphatidylserine for six months, with neuropsychological testing, EEG and PET measurement before and after [6][7]. A randomised double-blind placebo-controlled trial in 120 geriatric patients with chronic brain syndrome ran for 12 weeks at 200 mg three times daily; 107 patients, 54 on pyritinol and 53 on placebo, were analysed on rating scales and performance tests [8]. A 1981 randomised trial in 270 patients with sequelae of head injury reported statistically significant improvement over placebo after six weeks [9].

In 12 healthy male volunteers, a randomised crossover study found improvements in critical flicker fusion and choice reaction time after three days of pyritinol, with no significant differences on other tests [10]. A 2009 randomised double-blind trial of 108 term babies with post-asphyxial encephalopathy, given pyritinol or placebo for six months, found no statistically significant difference in mental or psychomotor development at one year [11]. A 1973 double-blind trial compared pyritinol with placebo for preventing alcohol hangover symptoms [12], and a 2022 systematic review of hangover interventions, in which no two studies tested the same intervention, rated efficacy outcomes as very low quality overall [13]. A 2014 randomised study examined vinpocetine and pyritinol together for blood rheology in cerebrovascular disorders [14], and pharmaco-EEG work has characterised effects on brain activity [15]. A 1993 European multicentre study compared it with auranofin in rheumatoid arthritis [1]. A registered pharmacovigilance study in 407 gerontopsychiatric patients was terminated [16]. No studies were found of pyritinol for appearance.

Nausea and headache are the common effects. Rarer reactions include mild skin allergy, acute pancreatitis and a photoallergic eruption, and a 2004 review of six case reports linked it to severe cholestatic hepatitis in patients also taking several other drugs [1]. Pyritinol is among drugs reported to induce pemphigus, a blistering skin disease, in dermatology case literature, including two cases of superficial pemphigus described in 1978 [17][18]. The geriatric trial reported no notable adverse reactions beyond those seen with placebo [8].

Wikipedia gives an elimination half-life of about 2.5 hours and does not describe a mechanism [1]. Grokipedia, an AI-generated source, describes effects on brain glucose metabolism and cholinergic activity in lab and animal work [19]. Lab studies have examined effects on GABA-synthesis enzymes, on diabetic-rat nociception and oxidative stress, and on oxidative DNA damage in human lymphocytes [20][21][22].

Merck produced pyritinol in 1961, and it entered European markets in the 1970s under brands such as Encephabol; a 1976 German clinical report discussed experience with Encephabol [1][23]. Since the early 1990s it has been available in the US as a dietary supplement [1]. Availability varies by country, from prescription to over-the-counter sale [1].
